blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Large language models offer a promising foundation for chemical reasoning,
bringing together chemical knowledge and multistep problem solving.
Chemical intuition can provide an initial sense of plausible outcomes
before the details of a solution are fully worked out.
Inspired by how such expectations complement explicit analysis, we study
how continuous latent thoughts can be trained to anticipate informative
aspects of future solutions without verbalizing every intermediate step. We introduce Latent-JEPA , a framework that combines autoregressive learning with
joint-embedding prediction of one or more future views. For chemical
reasoning, we develop textual and molecular prediction objectives that
connect latent thoughts to both subsequent reasoning and molecular outcomes.
Experiments on ChemCoTBench show gains in molecular
optimization and on several editing and reaction metrics. Representation
analyses show that future prediction makes latent thoughts more informative
about molecular outcomes and strengthens their correspondence with chemical
structure. These findings support abstract future prediction as a learning
principle for connecting continuous latent reasoning with scientific outcomes.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Scientific discovery often begins before a complete explanation is available. Researchers form hypotheses, recognize promising directions, and develop expectations about possible outcomes while important details remain unresolved. This interplay between provisional understanding and explicit analysis has long been discussed in accounts of scientific reasoning. Poincaré and Maitland (2003) emphasized the complementary roles of intuition and logical demonstration in mathematical
invention, while Polanyi and Sen (2009) argued that scientific
knowledge contains an important tacit component that cannot always be fully
articulated. Cognitive studies likewise suggest that
people can become sensitive to meaningful coherence before they can explicitly
identify it ( Bowers et al., 1990 ) .
Such expectations do not replace formal reasoning or empirical validation;
they help identify and organize possibilities that can subsequently be
worked out and tested. For scientific reasoning models ( Truhn et al., 2023 ; Narayanan et al., 2026 ; Pang et al., 2026 ) , such anticipatory structure could complement the explicit multistep reasoning already used in scientific problem solving. We ask how a scientific reasoning model might learn
an analogous capability: forming useful expectations about a solution before
that solution is fully articulated.

blocks.en:
In chemistry, intuition can provide an initial sense of plausible outcomes before the details of a solution are fully worked out. An experienced chemist
may, for example, have an initial sense of what transformations are plausible
or how a change in molecular structure might affect an outcome before working
through all of the details. Such judgments draw on accumulated chemical
knowledge and patterns learned through experience ( Talanquer, 2022 ) . They complement explicit analysis and can be
refined and tested as reasoning proceeds. We draw inspiration from this
anticipatory aspect of chemical intuition to study how models can learn useful
expectations about future solutions.

blocks.en:
Continuous latent reasoning provides a computational setting in which to
study this idea. Chain-of-thought (CoT) expresses intermediate reasoning in
language ( Wei et al., 2022 ) , whereas continuous reasoning allows models to
update internal thoughts without verbalizing every step. Coconut implements
hidden-state feedback ( Hao et al., 2024 ) , CODI learns continuous reasoning
through self-distillation ( Shen et al., 2025 ) , and LatentChem incorporates
dynamic molecular representations into chemical latent reasoning ( Ye et al., 2026 ) .
We ask a complementary learning question: can predicting representations of future solutions improve both
the information retained in latent thoughts and the reasoning they support?

blocks.en:
An informative prediction need not specify every detail of what comes next.
When a glass tips over the edge of a table, one may anticipate that it could
break without predicting the position of every shard ( Battaglia et al., 2013 ) .
Similarly, an improvising poet may be guided by an implicit sense of
rhyme without explicitly planning the line in advance.
These examples motivate studying how internal representations can
anticipate meaningful aspects of a future before its full realization.
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a learning principle
aligned with this distinction: predict an encoded view rather than reconstruct
its observable details ( Dawid and LeCun, 2024 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) .
Predictive video models have also shown sensitivity to violations of physical
expectations ( Garrido et al., 2025 ) .
For continuous reasoning, this motivates training latent thoughts to predict
representations of subsequent reasoning and outcomes, while leaving their
explicit realization to autoregressive generation.

blocks.en:
We introduce Latent-JEPA , which augments continuous latent reasoning with
joint-embedding prediction of future representations. The reasoner determines how latent computation unfolds, while future views specify what aspects of a developing solution it is trained to anticipate. For chemical reasoning, we
instantiate this principle with two complementary views. A textual view
represents the remaining reasoning and answer in the language model’s
representation space, while a molecular view uses a pretrained molecular
encoder to represent the chemical outcome ( Soares et al., 2025 ) . The two views
capture different aspects of the same solution: different explanations can
describe the same molecular outcome, and similar forms of reasoning can lead
to different structures. A shared latent thought predicts both views in their
respective spaces, allowing linguistic and chemical outcomes to provide
complementary supervision without requiring a common target representation.

blocks.en: We evaluate Latent-JEPA on ChemCoTBench ( Hao et al., 2026 ) . Latent-JEPA improves molecular optimization and several editing and reaction metrics. Our analyses further show that predictive supervision makes individual molecular outcomes more recoverable from latent thoughts and brings recurrent representations into closer correspondence with molecular structure. Together, these results support abstract future prediction as a way to train latent thoughts to form useful expectations about future reasoning and chemical outcomes before explicit generation. More broadly, Latent-JEPA takes a step toward the anticipatory aspect of scientific intuition, where internal computation forms useful expectations about possible outcomes before an explicit solution is produced.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Predictive representation learning. Predictive representation learning provides a way to supervise abstractions
of an observation. JEPA predicts embeddings of withheld views rather than
reconstructing their low-level details ( Dawid and LeCun, 2024 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) .
Related non-contrastive methods study target asymmetry and representation
collapse ( Grill et al., 2020 ; Bardes et al., 2021 ) , while LLM-JEPA combines
embedding prediction with language modeling ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
Future Summary Prediction and Semformer extend prediction to representations
of a future text segment ( Mahajan et al., 2026 ; Yin et al., 2024 ) .
We apply this principle to thoughts produced during continuous reasoning,
with language and molecular representations describing complementary futures.

blocks.en:
We aim to train latent thoughts to form useful expectations about a
solution before it is fully expressed. To this end, Latent-JEPA combines
autoregressive learning with prediction of representations of subsequent
reasoning and outcomes ( Figure 1 ). Let W t W_{t} denote the reasoner’s current workspace
and h t h_{t} a continuous representation of intermediate reasoning read
from that workspace: W 0 = I θ ​ ( x ) , h t = R θ ​ ( W t ) , W t + 1 = U θ ​ ( W t , h t ) . W_{0}=I_{\theta}(x),\qquad h_{t}=R_{\theta}(W_{t}),\qquad W_{t+1}=U_{\theta}(W_{t},h_{t}). (1) Here x x is the input, I θ I_{\theta} initializes the workspace, R θ R_{\theta} reads
the thought, and U θ U_{\theta} advances the reasoning process for 0 ≤ t < K 0\leq t<K .
A decoder generates the answer from W K W_{K} . The workspace can include the
reasoner’s attention cache or domain-specific state, allowing this formulation
to cover different continuous reasoning architectures.

A Latent-JEPA architecture consists of a continuous latent reasoner and, at
each supervised step t ∈ ℐ ⊆ { 0 , … , K } t\in\mathcal{I}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,K\} , a finite family
of future-view maps, target encoders, and predictors { ( ϕ t , j , E j , P j ) } j = 1 N t \{(\phi_{t,j},E_{j},P_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N_{t}} , where N t ≥ 1 N_{t}\geq 1 .
Given a reference continuation or outcome F > t F_{>t} available during
training, ϕ t , j \phi_{t,j} selects a future view, E j E_{j} encodes it,
and P j P_{j} predicts its representation from h t h_{t} : v t , j = ϕ t , j ​ ( F > t ) , z t , j = E j ​ ( v t , j ) , z ^ t , j = P j ​ ( h t , q t , j ) , v_{t,j}=\phi_{t,j}(F_{>t}),\qquad z_{t,j}=E_{j}(v_{t,j}),\qquad\widehat{z}_{t,j}=P_{j}(h_{t},q_{t,j}), (2) where q t , j q_{t,j} optionally specifies a prediction horizon or query.
The latent thought h t h_{t} depends only on computation preceding the future
view. Each predictor maps the thought into its target encoder’s representation
space, where a discrepancy d j ​ ( z ^ t , j , z t , j ) d_{j}(\widehat{z}_{t,j},z_{t,j}) supplies the
predictive learning signal.

A future view can describe an intermediate reasoning step, the answer, or a
domain-specific outcome. Different views can use different encoders and
representation spaces; multiple horizons can also share an encoder and a
query-conditioned predictor. The framework leaves these choices open so that
new target representations and reasoning architectures can extend the same
predictive structure.
The definition also leaves the use of the components after training open.
Encoders and predictors may support downstream planning or evaluation using
information available at inference. In this work, we use the predictive branches to supervise latent thoughts
during training, without changing the reasoner’s generation procedure.

blocks.en: 3.1 Target asymmetry and geometry

blocks.en:
The target branch observes information withheld from the latent thought.
Stop-gradient makes the prediction asymmetric: the predictor and reasoner
learn to approach the target representation without directly optimizing the
target through the same loss. When encoder parameters are shared with the
reasoner, they still evolve through autoregressive and prediction-side
updates. A frozen encoder instead provides a fixed representation space.
Target geometry also determines which prediction errors are informative.
If embeddings share a dominant common direction, high cosine similarity may
reveal little about the corresponding example. We center target representations
using means estimated from training data and apply ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization
to expose variation across examples. We evaluate
this geometry through pairwise similarity and effective rank, and test
sample-specific prediction using shuffled targets. These are diagnostic
controls; the training objective in Equation 3 is non-contrastive.

agreement with Morgan fingerprints, which are not used as prediction targets. These results suggest that structure-native future targets can shape recurrent representations toward molecular relationships that extend beyond the target space itself. More generally, the choice of JEPA target determines which aspects of a future solution the latent state is encouraged to emphasize.

blocks.en: Discussion. Our results suggest a computational perspective on intuitive reasoning in continuous latent models. Scientific intuition often involves forming an expectation of a plausible outcome before the details of a solution are fully worked out; LATENT-JEPA instantiates this idea by training latent computation to anticipate abstract representations of future reasoning and outcomes before explicit generation. The representation analyses show that such supervision makes molecular outcomes more accessible from latent thoughts and reshapes recurrent computation toward chemically meaningful structure, suggesting that intermediate states can be trained not only to support eventual token generation, but also to encode useful expectations about what comes next. From this perspective, the choice of prediction target determines which aspects of the future are emphasized, while the predictive objective provides a more general mechanism for shaping the internal computation that precedes generation. More broadly, future prediction may influence not only what information is present in individual latent thoughts, but also how latent thoughts evolve through recurrent computation and how the underlying latent manifold is organized around possible future outcomes. Understanding these dynamics may provide a useful path toward intuitive reasoning in scientific models, where useful expectations emerge before a solution is explicitly worked out. Future work can further study how such latent trajectories develop across reasoning depth and whether different stages of computation benefit from different prediction horizons or levels of abstraction.
blocks.zh: 讨论。 我们的结果显示,对连续潜伏模型中的直觉推理有一个计算视角。 科学直觉往往涉及在充分制定解决方案的细节之前形成一种可能的结果的预期;LATENT-JEPA通过培训潜在的计算,在明确生成之前预测未来推理和结果的抽象表述,从而将这一想法迅速化为现实。 表现分析显示,这种监督使得分子结果更容易从潜伏的思想中获取,并将经常性的计算重塑为具有化学意义的结构,这表明中间状态不仅可以被训练支持最终的象征性生成,还可以编码对接下来的事物的有用期望. 从这个角度来说,预测目标的选择决定了未来哪些方面受到强调,而预测目标则为塑造在生成之前的内部计算提供了更普遍的机制. 更广泛地说,未来的预测不仅可能影响个人潜伏思想中的信息,而且还会影响潜伏思想如何通过反复计算而演变,以及潜伏的多元性如何围绕未来可能的结果来组织。 了解这些动态可能为科学模型的直观推理提供一条有益的道路,在明确制定解决办法之前,就会产生有益的期望。 今后的工作可以进一步研究这种潜在的轨迹如何跨越推理深度发展,以及不同的计算阶段是否受益于不同的预测视野或抽象程度。

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced Latent-JEPA , a framework for learning latent thoughts through
prediction of future representations. Its formulation connects a continuous
reasoner to one or more future views and allows different encoders and
predictors to define the supervision. In chemistry, we train latent thoughts
to anticipate both the remaining reasoning and molecular outcomes.
Experiments show gains in chemical task performance and stronger molecular
information in latent thoughts. These findings motivate future prediction as
a learning objective for continuous reasoning and open further study of how
future representations can guide reasoning and planning.

用于定义监管的预测器。 在化学中,我们培养潜伏的思想
以预测剩余的推理结果和分子结果。
实验显示在化学任务性能和较强分子方面有所收获
潜在思想中的信息。 这些结论促使今后预测:
持续推理的学习目标,并公开进一步研究如何

blocks.en:
Textual prediction improves 10 of 17 metrics over Vanilla Coconut, with
four regressions and three ties; molecular and dual prediction
improve seven and eight metrics, respectively. Textual prediction has the lowest average rank in this comparison,
while molecular and dual prediction favor different tasks. For example,
molecular prediction performs best on DRD2 and GSK3- β \beta , while dual
prediction performs best on QED and Murcko similarity. These results show
that predictive supervision can benefit a model whose molecular inputs are
provided only as text. The different patterns in Coconut-Chem and Vanilla
Coconut motivate choosing future views together with the task and reasoning
setup; their source interfaces, initialization, and training histories are
not otherwise matched. Appendix H examines the associated
representation patterns within each setting.

blocks.en: The average probe gains leave open whether the improvement is widespread or concentrated in a few examples. We examine this distribution, then study how prediction and structural agreement vary across tasks and recurrent depth. For probing, we fit a separate ridge map at each step using 1,224 training examples and evaluate it on 321 molecular-target-eligible ChemCoTBench test examples. We compare corresponding targets with a fixed within-task permutation of evaluation targets. The probes use latent hidden states, whereas RSA uses recurrent feedback embeddings. SMI-TED RSA uses the same 321 test examples, and Morgan RSA uses the subset of 294 with valid outcome fingerprints; Appendix K specifies the protocols and depth indexing.
blocks.zh: 平均探查收益是普遍改善还是集中在几个例子中,都没有定论。 我们审查这种分布,然后研究预测和结构一致如何因任务和反复发生的深度而异。 为了进行探测,我们利用1 224个训练实例,在每一步骤上都安装一个单独的山脊图,并在321个分子目标合格ChemCoTBench试验实例上加以评价。 我们把相应的目标与固定的任务内评价目标进行比较。 探测器使用潜在的隐藏状态,而RSA则使用经常性的反馈嵌入. SMI-TED RSA使用相同的321个测试示例,摩根RSA使用294的子集,并带有有效的结果指纹;附录K指定协议和深度索引.

Molecular understanding and scaffold abstraction. Functional-group and ring-counting tasks ask the model to identify structural
features of an input molecule; we report mean absolute count error.
The Murcko task asks for the molecule’s scaffold, the core formed by its

prediction and reference: identical scaffolds score one; otherwise it uses

Forward-reaction prediction. Given the reaction inputs, the model predicts either the major product or
the byproduct. We report fingerprint Tanimoto similarity (FTS) to the
reference outcome and the fraction of chemically parseable outputs
(validity), separately for the two tasks.
FTS is the arithmetic mean of Tanimoto similarities computed using RDKit
topological, MACCS-key, and radius-two Morgan count fingerprints. These
encode paths, predefined structural features, and local atom neighborhoods,
respectively. Higher FTS indicates greater structural similarity on a
zero-to-one scale. This three-fingerprint score differs from the Morgan-only
comparison used for RSA in Section K.3 . Outputs that RDKit cannot
parse as molecules receive zero similarity and remain in the denominator.
